blocks.content: They both have "design" in the name, and they both involve thinking hard before writing code. But they operate at completely different altitudes and confusing the two is one of the most common mistakes engineers make in interviews and on the job.
1. Two Levels of Design Thinking
blocks.text: 1. Two Levels of Design Thinking

blocks.content: Think of a city. A city planner looks at the whole map where the highways go, which zones are residential versus commercial, how the water mains connect neighbourhoods. They never zoom into one house. That's High Level Design.

Now think of an architect hired to design one of those houses. They decide where every wall sits, how the plumbing routes from the main, how many outlets each room gets, what load-bearing beams are needed. They never look at the city map. That's Low Level Design.
Both are essential. Neither can replace the other. And critically you can't do the second one well without the first one being done first.

HIGH LEVEL DESIGN

The city planner's view

Sees the whole system at once. Decides which services exist, how they connect, how data flows between them, and what happens at scale.

Output: architecture diagrams, service maps, technology stack decisions.

LOW LEVEL DESIGN

The architect's view

Zooms into one component. Decides how it's structured internally the classes, interfaces, methods, and logic that make it work.

Output: class diagrams, code structure, design pattern choices.

blocks.content: 2. Side by side: every dimension compared
blocks.text: 2. Side by side: every dimension compared

blocks.content: The clearest way to understand the difference is to look at the same question through both lenses. Here's how HLD and LLD approach every major design dimension differently.

{"headers":["Dimension","High Level Design","Low Level Design"],"rows":[["Focus","What systems exist and how they communicate","How one system works on the inside"],["Zoom level","Bird's eye — whole system at once","Ground level: one component at a time"],["Key decisions","Microservices vs monolith, SQL vs NoSQL, sync vs async","Class structure, design patterns, method signatures"],["Output","Architecture diagram, service map, data flow","Class diagram, code skeleton, interface contracts"],["Concerns","Scalability, fault tolerance, latency, cost","Extensibility, testability, maintainability, SOLID"],["Audience","Architects, tech leads, stakeholders","Engineers building and maintaining the component"],["Happens when","Before any component is built","Before each component's code is written"]]}
The best way to feel the difference is to look at one real problem through both lenses. Let's design a food delivery app from both perspectives.
Example: Food Delivery App
blocks.text: Example: Food Delivery App

blocks.content:
HLD asks: What services do we need? How does an order flow from the customer's phone to the restaurant to the driver's app? 

Should we use a message queue between services? Which database scales best for menu data? What happens if the notification service goes down?

LLD asks: Inside the Order service, what does the Order class look like? What's the interface for PaymentProcessor? 

How does RideMatcher decide which driver to assign? What design pattern should NotificationService use so adding WhatsApp notifications later doesn't require rewriting it?

blocks.content: 3. When does each happen?
blocks.text: 3. When does each happen?

blocks.content: HLD and LLD are not interchangeable phases they're sequential. You cannot do meaningful LLD until HLD has answered the big structural questions.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512511483-108582535.png
blocks.alt: Flow diagram showing HLD happening first, then LLD per component, with a feedback loop back to HLD when component design reveals a problem

blocks.content: 1. HLD happens first
blocks.text: 1. HLD happens first

blocks.content: Before writing a single class, you need to know what services exist, how they communicate, and what each one is responsible for. Jumping into LLD without HLD is like designing a room before knowing which floor of the building it's on.
2. LLD happens per component
blocks.text: 2. LLD happens per component

blocks.content: Once HLD is settled, LLD is done for each service or module separately. The Order service gets its own LLD. The Notification service gets its own LLD. They happen in parallel once the contracts between services are agreed.
3. They inform each other
blocks.text: 3. They inform each other

blocks.content: LLD sometimes reveals that an HLD decision was wrong. If designing the Order service class structure shows that one service is doing too many things, that's feedback to go back and split it at the HLD level. Design is iterative, not linear.
4. What each one gets wrong without the other
blocks.text: 4. What each one gets wrong without the other

blocks.content: HLD and LLD are two halves of the same discipline. Drop either one and the project suffers in predictable ways.
GREAT HLD, NO LLD
blocks.text: GREAT HLD, NO LLD

blocks.content: The architecture looks beautiful on a whiteboard. Services are well-defined, APIs are clean, scalability is planned for.
But when engineers start building, there's no shared understanding of how classes should be structured.
Every developer makes different decisions. The codebase becomes inconsistent, untestable, and hard to extend. Technical debt piles up from day one.
GREAT LLD, NO HLD
blocks.text: GREAT LLD, NO HLD

blocks.content: The code inside each component is beautiful. Clean classes, perfect SOLID adherence, elegant design patterns.

But the components don't connect well. Services duplicate logic. The database schema can't handle the scale. The system works in isolation but breaks as a whole. Beautiful code solving the wrong problem.
THE RIGHT MENTAL MODEL: HLD ensures you're building the right system. LLD ensures you're building the system right. You need both in that order.
blocks.text: THE RIGHT MENTAL MODEL: HLD ensures you're building the right system. LLD ensures you're building the system right. You need both in that order.

blocks.content: 5. In interviews: what each round tests
blocks.text: 5. In interviews: what each round tests

blocks.content: Companies test HLD and LLD in separate rounds because they test completely different skills. Knowing which one you're in changes everything about how you should approach the problem.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512514615-412098671.png
blocks.alt: Diagram contrasting the design Twitter prompt which leads to an HLD round versus the design a parking lot prompt which leads to an LLD round

blocks.content: If they say "design Twitter": That's HLD. Think load balancers, CDN, fanout strategies, database sharding. Don't dive into class design.
If they say "design a parking lot": That's LLD. Think classes likeParkingSpot,Vehicle,Ticket. Don't draw architecture diagrams.
HLD interview signals: They ask about scale, failure scenarios, data volume, global distribution, and tech choices.
LLD interview signals: They ask to "write the classes", "show the relationships", "apply OOP principles", "which design pattern fits here".

COMMON INTERVIEW MISTAKE: Candidates in an LLD round start drawing service boxes and load balancers. Candidates in an HLD round start sketching class diagrams. Both immediately signal a misunderstanding of the question. Always confirm which layer the interviewer wants before you start.
blocks.text: COMMON INTERVIEW MISTAKE: Candidates in an LLD round start drawing service boxes and load balancers. Candidates in an HLD round start sketching class diagrams. Both immediately signal a misunderstanding of the question. Always confirm which layer the interviewer wants before you start.

blocks.content: 6. Worked Example: A URL Shortener At Both Levels
blocks.text: 6. Worked Example: A URL Shortener At Both Levels

blocks.content: Food delivery is a big system with a lot of moving parts. Let's use a smaller, more focused example so the contrast between HLD and LLD is even sharper: a URL shortener, the kind of service that turns a long link into something like algo.xl/a1B2c3.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512516389-286552815.png
blocks.alt: Diagram showing the URL shortener zoomed out at HLD as one box, then zoomed into that box to reveal the LLD classes inside it

blocks.content: HLD view: URL shortener
blocks.text: HLD view: URL shortener

blocks.content: At the high level, nobody is thinking about classes yet. The questions are about traffic, storage, and how requests move through the system.

["API gateway: accepts create and redirect requests, applies rate limiting.","Shortening service: a stateless service that turns a long URL into a short key.","Key value store or cache such as Redis: serves redirects fast without hitting the primary database every time.","Primary database: durable storage mapping short keys to long URLs, chosen for high read throughput.","Analytics pipeline: a separate async path that logs click events without slowing down the redirect itself."]
items: API gateway: accepts create and redirect requests, applies rate limiting.
Shortening service: a stateless service that turns a long URL into a short key.
Key value store or cache such as Redis: serves redirects fast without hitting the primary database every time.
Primary database: durable storage mapping short keys to long URLs, chosen for high read throughput.
Analytics pipeline: a separate async path that logs click events without slowing down the redirect itself.

blocks.content: The HLD conversation is entirely about read heavy traffic (redirects vastly outnumber new link creations), so the design leans on caching and read replicas. There is no mention yet of what a class looks like inside the shortening service, that decision belongs one layer down.
LLD view: URL shortener
blocks.text: LLD view: URL shortener

blocks.content: Once HLD has settled that the shortening service exists and talks to a cache and a database, LLD takes over and asks: what classes live inside that one box, and how do they collaborate?

Two decisions dominate the LLD conversation here. First, how is the short key actually generated, base62 encoding of an incrementing counter is one common approach. Second, how is storage abstracted so the service does not care whether it is backed by Redis, DynamoDB, or an in memory map during tests.

Notice what changed between the two levels. The KeyGenerationStrategy interface and the UrlRepository interface never appear in the HLD conversation, and the cache, the API gateway, and the analytics pipeline never appear inside this class diagram. Each level intentionally hides the other's details.

7. Design Patterns Live At Different Altitudes
blocks.text: 7. Design Patterns Live At Different Altitudes

blocks.content: Both HLD and LLD reuse "patterns", proven solutions to recurring problems, but the patterns that show up at each layer are almost entirely different, and mixing them up is a common tell that someone has not worked at both levels.
Patterns you will meet in HLD discussions
blocks.text: Patterns you will meet in HLD discussions

blocks.content: These are architectural patterns. They describe how whole services, databases, and networks behave under load.

["Load balancing strategies: round robin, least connections, consistent hashing.","Cache aside and write through caching for reducing database load.","Circuit breaker: stopping calls to a failing downstream service before it takes the whole system down.","Database sharding and replication for scaling storage horizontally.","Event driven patterns like CQRS and event sourcing for decoupling writes from reads.","API gateway and service mesh patterns for routing traffic between services."]
items: Load balancing strategies: round robin, least connections, consistent hashing.
Cache aside and write through caching for reducing database load.
Circuit breaker: stopping calls to a failing downstream service before it takes the whole system down.
Database sharding and replication for scaling storage horizontally.
Event driven patterns like CQRS and event sourcing for decoupling writes from reads.
API gateway and service mesh patterns for routing traffic between services.

blocks.content: Patterns you will meet in LLD discussions
blocks.text: Patterns you will meet in LLD discussions

blocks.content: These are the classic Gang of Four object oriented design patterns. They describe how classes inside one component collaborate.

["Strategy: swap an algorithm, such as the key generation logic above, without changing the caller.","Factory: centralize object creation so callers do not need to know concrete classes.","Observer: let one object notify many listeners without knowing who they are, as seen in the NotificationService below.","Singleton: ensure exactly one instance of a class exists, useful for a shared configuration object.","Decorator: attach new behaviour to an object at runtime without subclassing.","State: change an object's behaviour when its internal state changes, common in order or ticket lifecycle classes."]
items: Strategy: swap an algorithm, such as the key generation logic above, without changing the caller.
Factory: centralize object creation so callers do not need to know concrete classes.
Observer: let one object notify many listeners without knowing who they are, as seen in the NotificationService below.
Singleton: ensure exactly one instance of a class exists, useful for a shared configuration object.
Decorator: attach new behaviour to an object at runtime without subclassing.
State: change an object's behaviour when its internal state changes, common in order or ticket lifecycle classes.

blocks.content: The rule of thumb: if the pattern is about network calls, databases, or servers, it is an HLD pattern. If the pattern is about objects, interfaces, and method calls inside one process, it is an LLD pattern.
Observer pattern in practice: a notification service
blocks.text: Observer pattern in practice: a notification service

blocks.content: Here is the same NotificationService mentioned earlier in the food delivery example, built out as a real LLD class design using the Observer pattern so a new channel can be added without touching existing code.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: Before this design, adding WhatsApp notifications would have meant editing an existing if/else chain inside NotificationService. After this design, it means writing one new class and calling subscribe. That is the entire point of LLD: decisions made here determine how painful every future change will be.
8. Switching Mental Gears Quickly
blocks.text: 8. Switching Mental Gears Quickly

blocks.content: In real projects and in interviews, you often have to move between these two modes within the same conversation. Here is a practical checklist for making that switch deliberately instead of by accident.

["If unsure which mode is expected, ask directly: \"Should I focus on the overall architecture or on the class design for one part of it?\"","Starting an HLD answer: open with scale numbers, requests per second, data size, read versus write ratio, before drawing anything.","Starting an LLD answer: open by listing the core nouns in the problem, the entities that will become classes, before writing any method.","While doing HLD, resist the urge to name a single method signature, that is premature.","While doing LLD, resist the urge to draw a load balancer or mention sharding, that is out of scope.","If you notice a class design forcing an awkward workaround, that is a signal to revisit the HLD decision, not to patch around it in code."]
items: If unsure which mode is expected, ask directly: "Should I focus on the overall architecture or on the class design for one part of it?"
Starting an HLD answer: open with scale numbers, requests per second, data size, read versus write ratio, before drawing anything.
Starting an LLD answer: open by listing the core nouns in the problem, the entities that will become classes, before writing any method.
While doing HLD, resist the urge to name a single method signature, that is premature.
While doing LLD, resist the urge to draw a load balancer or mention sharding, that is out of scope.
If you notice a class design forcing an awkward workaround, that is a signal to revisit the HLD decision, not to patch around it in code.

blocks.content: HLD decides which boxes exist and how they talk. LLD decides what happens inside one box. Confusing the two wastes time in both directions.
9. Quick Recap
blocks.text: 9. Quick Recap

blocks.content: {"headers":["Question","HLD","LLD"],"rows":[["What is being designed","The whole system, its services and their connections","One component, its classes and their collaborations"],["Typical artifact","Architecture diagram","Class diagram or code skeleton"],["Typical interview prompt","Design Twitter, design an e commerce checkout","Design a parking lot, design a rate limiter class"],["Comes first or second","First, it sets the boundaries","Second, it fills in each boundary"],["Failure mode without it","Beautiful code with no coherent system around it","A clean architecture full of tangled, unmaintainable classes"]]}

If you remember one sentence from this entire lesson, make it this: HLD decides what to build and how the pieces fit together, LLD decides how to build each piece well. Every topic in this course from here on is teaching you the LLD half, so keep asking yourself, as you go, which box would this class actually live inside.
